episode.throughLine: A short retrospective account of writing while unemployed, revising an older manuscript while two others circulated, and receiving an acceptance alongside a rejection.

contentProfile.contentNote: Job loss, fear of failure and publication refusals. FOR OWNER READING under the user-authorized short source-led format, not approval. Period summaries replace unlocated scenes; no acceptance-day reaction is invented. Ends at the 1975 sale, excluding the prior draft's 1976 travel coda. Ages 27–28; matching unchanged.

facts.statement: Butler recalled crying at her layoff.

sourceRefs.locator: Paragraph about the final job loss immediately before the account of assembling Patternmaster; Butler's first-person statement, not the reporter's reconstruction.

facts.statement: Octavia E. Butler recalled being twenty-seven, laid off, supported by unemployment compensation and afraid that her writing would never succeed.

sourceRefs.locator: Final answer, paragraph beginning 'I was able to find the time'.

facts.statement: Butler recalled rising at two or three in the morning to write before office, factory or warehouse work; she disliked the jobs, left jobs and found others, and accumulated rejections.
Butler recalled throwing away all her accumulated rejection slips one day in disgust.
At eighteen Butler won a college writing contest and received fifteen dollars, her first money from writing; at twenty-three she sold two short stories to writers teaching at Clarion.
Butler said only one of those two stories was published, and she sold no other writing for five years before selling her first novel.
Butler feared that relatives urging a civil-service job might be right; she remembered feeling desperate during the period of unemployment-supported novel writing.
While those two novels were under consideration, Butler began revising Survivor, an old novel begun in her teens.
While working on Survivor, Butler received a rejection of Mind of My Mind and an acceptance of Patternmaster; she did not specify the delivery medium, day, order or her physical reaction.

sourceRefs.locator: Final answer, paragraph beginning 'And while I was working on Survivor'.

facts.statement: Butler said she sold Patternmaster in 1975 and it was published in 1976.
Octavia E. Butler was a science-fiction novelist and the author of Patternmaster.

arc.canonicalText: She was twenty-seven when she lost her job. In her memory, she cried at the layoff. Unemployment payments then gave her time to write. She was trying to sell a novel.
arc.sourceNote: Retrospective event and ensuing period, not a located layoff scene. Short source-led vignette authorized 2026-09-20; FOR OWNER READING, not approved.

arc.canonicalText: She feared that nothing would come of her writing. Her relatives thought she should find a steady government job. She worried that they were right. The available writing time had not removed that fear.
arc.sourceNote: An attested period-level fear; no representative anxious night or room is staged. Short source-led vignette authorized 2026-09-20; FOR OWNER READING, not approved.

arc.canonicalText: While two novels were with publishers, she returned to an older manuscript. She had begun it in her teens. She started revising it.
arc.sourceNote: A documented work-period action, not an invented immediate layoff response. The composition order of the other novels is not asserted. Short source-led vignette authorized 2026-09-20; FOR OWNER READING, not approved.

arc.canonicalText: Before this, she had fitted writing around paid work. She rose early to write before leaving for offices, factories or warehouses. Rejection slips accumulated. One day, disgusted, she threw them away. Earlier, she had sold two stories at a workshop. Only one appeared. Five years passed without another sale.
arc.sourceNote: Explicit backward summary. Rejections and the long sales gap are real; their exact placement within individual revision sessions is not manufactured. Short source-led vignette authorized 2026-09-20; FOR OWNER READING, not approved.

arc.canonicalText: During the revision, one publisher refused a novel and another accepted her first book. Both replies belonged to that period. The acceptance did not make the other refusal disappear.
arc.sourceNote: Two outcomes in a remembered period, not two letters arriving together. Exact day, order, medium and reaction are unknown. Authorized vignette exception. Short source-led vignette authorized 2026-09-20; FOR OWNER READING, not approved.

arc.canonicalText: She had made her first novel sale. The long gap after the short stories had ended. One manuscript had found a publisher; another had been refused. Not every answer was yes.
arc.sourceNote: Ends at the 1975 sale. Publication and vacation in 1976 are excluded from the narrative; no promised livelihood or emotional recovery. Short source-led vignette authorized 2026-09-20; FOR OWNER READING, not approved.

arc.canonicalText:
Her name was Octavia Butler.

She wrote science-fiction novels.

Your life is not theirs.

But a piece of this story may still sit beside you.

You do not have to turn one answer into a judgment of everything.

You are allowed to have mixed feelings.
arc.sourceNote: Identity and permission only; no advice to persist, leave work or rely on writing for income. Short source-led vignette authorized 2026-09-20; FOR OWNER READING, not approved.

dramatizationLimits: No invented layoff room, letter-opening action, acceptance-day feeling or single-day pairing of replies.
Retrospective accounts stay probable and briefly framed as memory.
Do not infer financial independence or a cure for fear from the first novel sale.
avoidRules: Do not date Amber's undated revision after the layoff; that material is omitted.
Do not resolve conflicting composition-order memories by silently choosing one.
Do not extend this narrowed narrative into the 1976 vacation.
The short source-led structure is an authorized exception, not a claim of full moment/length recipe compliance.
